Image: byoa: your users bring their own agent. byoa lets your app run each user's own Claude Code or Codex, on their plan and with their tools, in any sandbox, from inside your own backend. # byoa: bring your own agent

**byoa lets your app run each user's own Claude Code or Codex, on their plan and with their tools, in any sandbox, from inside your own backend.**

byoa is an open-source library that helps you build AI-native apps fast. Your app runs the user's own Claude Code or Codex in a sandbox. The user signs in with their own ChatGPT or Claude plan, so they pay for the AI work with a plan they already have. The user connects each MCP tool (Notion, Gmail, and others) one time, and every agent run has it.

Version 1 supports three sandbox providers: E2B, Daytona and Instabox. More providers come later. To change the provider, you change one adapter.

## Who brings what

**Your app brings the product. Each user brings the agent.** You build the app and pick the sandbox. Each user brings their plan and their tools. byoa runs inside your backend and runs each job in that user's own sandbox.

Image: Who brings what: you, the developer, build the app, pick the sandbox provider and own the database, and import byoa into your app's backend. The end user uses the app, signs in on the lab's own page and connects each MCP tool once. Your app code calls agents.run on byoa, which keeps AI logins and MCP grants in your database. byoa's box reaches past your backend's edge: outside it, byoa creates, runs and destroys a sandbox for each job at E2B or Daytona on your account, where the user's own Claude Code or Codex runs; the AI labs get the model calls, paid by the user's own plan; and the user's MCP servers get the real token from byoa's proxy.

The same diagram as text

```text
DEVELOPER · YOU                                           END USER
┌────────────────────────────────────┐                    ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│ builds the app                     │                    │ uses the app                       │
│ picks the sandbox provider         │                    │ has a Claude or ChatGPT plan       │
│ owns the database                  │                    │ has MCP tools and skills           │
└──────────────────┬─────────────────┘                    └──────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                   │ imports byoa             signs in on the lab's own page │
                   │                             connects each MCP tool once │
                   ▼                                                         ▼
┌─ YOUR APP'S BACKEND · you run it ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  your app code                                            your database                      │
│        │ agents.run(userId, task)                               ▲ AI logins, MCP grants      │
│        ▼                                                        │                            │
│ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┻━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ │
│ ┃ byoa · open source, Apache 2.0                                                           ┃ │
│ ┃   AI login · harness            skills · AGENTS.md            MCP OAuth · proxy          ┃ │
│ ┃              │                                                           │               ┃ │
└─╂┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄ ▲ your backend · outside it ▼ ┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄│┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄┄╂─┘
  ┃              │ create · run · destroy                         real token │               ┃
  ┃              ▼                                                           ▼               ┃
  ┃ ┌─ SANDBOX ────────────────┐  ┌─ AI LABS ────────────────┐  ┌─ MCP SERVERS ────────────┐ ┃
  ┃ │ E2B or Daytona,          │  │ Anthropic · OpenAI       │  │ Notion · Gmail · …       │ ┃
  ┃ │ on your account          ├─▶│ model calls, paid by     │  │ the user's own accounts  │ ┃
  ┃ │ runs the user's own      │  │ the user's own plan      │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ │ Claude Code or Codex     │  │                          │  │                          │ ┃
  ┃ └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘ ┃
  ┃                                                                                          ┃
  ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
```

## The problem

To make an app AI-native, you run a big lab's harness (Claude Code or Codex) in a sandbox, with the user's own AI plan. For each app, you must build the same connection layer again:

- the user's AI login, through the real CLI;
- the user's MCP connections and their OAuth tokens, with one refresh owner;
- the user's skills and AGENTS.md;
- the harness install and its updates;
- the code that connects all of this to one sandbox provider.

byoa is that layer, as a library, so you do not build it again for each app.

## What byoa is, and what it is not

- byoa **is** a library. It runs inside your app's own backend (Node or Convex). Cloudflare Workers support is planned.
- byoa **stores tokens in your own database**, through a store adapter.
- byoa **is not** a hosted service. We do not run a server, and we never see your users' tokens.

Image: What version 1 covers. Agents: Claude Code and Codex (v1), Gemini or Antigravity maybe later. User plans: Claude and ChatGPT (v1). Sandboxes: E2B, Daytona and Instabox (v1), other providers planned. Backends: Node and Convex actions (v1), Cloudflare Workers planned. Token stores: Convex and Postgres (v1), or your own with get, put, delete and compare-and-set.

## Why byoa

### The user's plan pays.

Each user signs in with their own Claude or ChatGPT plan, on Anthropic's or OpenAI's own sign-in page. The agent work runs on that plan, not on your API bill.

### The real agents.

Your app runs the real, unmodified Claude Code and Codex. Users get the full harness, with their tools and skills.

### Any sandbox.

Each sandbox provider is one adapter with one interface. E2B, Daytona and Instabox come first. To change the provider, you change one line.

### Connect once.

The user connects each MCP tool one time. Every agent run has it. The real tokens never go into the sandbox.

## How it works

byoa sits in your backend, between your users and their agents. Your app calls `agents.run(userId, task)`. byoa starts or resumes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, and runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan.

Image: Architecture: the end user, with a Claude or ChatGPT plan and Notion, Gmail and Heptabase accounts, uses your app. byoa runs inside your app's own backend: sandbox adapters (E2B, Daytona), the AI login flow (the real claude and codex CLI), a pinned harness installer, MCP OAuth with one refresh owner, skills and config, one event stream for both harnesses, the token store and the MCP proxy. It creates, runs and destroys the sandbox, where the unmodified Claude Code or Codex calls the AI labs on the user's own plan. As an option, the user's login is a volume mounted into the sandbox (cliLogin) instead of in the database. MCP calls go through the proxy to the MCP servers.

### Real tokens never go into the sandbox

The agent in the sandbox gets a short-lived job token. The proxy in your backend adds the real MCP token to each request.

Image: Token flow: the harness in the sandbox has an mcp.json that points to your proxy, with a job token for one job and one user, and no real MCP token. The MCP proxy in your backend checks the job token, adds the real token from the token store (your database, your key), sends the request on to the MCP server, and refuses the job token after the job ends.

### The sandbox of each job

Image: Lifecycle: 1. Create: byoa starts a sandbox at your provider. 2. Load the setup: pinned harness, skills, AGENTS.md and MCP config. 3. Run the job: text, tool calls and permission requests stream back as events. 4. Destroy: byoa destroys the sandbox at the provider. The user's AI login and MCP grants stay between jobs.

The picture shows `sandboxPer: 'job'`. By default, step 1 resumes the user's sandbox from the last job (or creates it for the first job), and step 4 pauses it.

## Install

byoa is not on npm yet. Until version 1, install it from GitHub:

```sh
npm install github:madeyexz/byoa     # npm builds it on install
bun add github:madeyexz/byoa        # Bun loads its TypeScript source
```

From version 1: `npm install byoa` or `bun add byoa`. For E2B, also install `e2b`. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun.

## Agent skill

[skills/byoa](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa) is a skill in the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format. It teaches a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Amp and others) to add byoa to an app: the install, `createAgents` with a store and a sandbox adapter, the sign-in, the MCP connections and their routes, `agents.run` and its events, and the lab rules. To install it in your app's repository:

```sh
npx skills add madeyexz/byoa              # Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others
amp skill add madeyexz/byoa/skills/byoa   # Amp
```

For LLMs, the site also serves the docs as [llms.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms.txt) (an index) and [llms-full.txt](https://byoa.rippling.computer/llms-full.txt) (the README, SPEC.md, the example and the skill in one file).

## How it will look

This is the API in this repository today. It can change before version 1.

```ts
import { createAgents } from 'byoa'
import { e2b } from 'byoa/sandbox/e2b'
import { postgresStore } from 'byoa/store/postgres'

const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp',                                    // one app's AI logins are only this app's
  sandbox: e2b({ apiKey }),
  store: postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }),
  encryptionKey,                                   // openssl rand -base64 32; grants and AI logins are encrypted with it
  proxyUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/mcp',  // serve agents.proxy here
  oauth: { redirectUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/callback' },
  tools: { todos: { add_todo: { description: 'Add one to-do.', input, run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, title) } } },  // your app's own tools
})

const claude = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'claude')  // { url }: Anthropic's own sign-in page
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'claude', { code })        // the code that page shows
const codex = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'codex')    // { url, code }: OpenAI's page and the code to enter
await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'codex', { waitMs: 60_000 })

const mcp = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
// mcp.signInUrl: the server's sign-in page; your redirectUrl route then calls agents.finishMcp({ state, code })

for await (const event of agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, mcp: ['notion', 'todos'], setup: { agentsMd, skills } })) {
  // start, text, tool_call, tool_result, permission, error, end: the same events for Claude Code and Codex
}
```

An app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness (for example its own server, which starts `claude` or `codex` itself) opens the job with `agents.session` instead. It gets the same sandbox, login, pinned harness and job token, and runs its own command:

```ts
const s = await agents.session(userId, { harness: 'claude', mcp: ['notion'] })
try {
  // s.bin: the pinned claude binary; s.env: its login folder, the job token and its MCP start timeout; s.mcp: [{ name, url }] at the proxy
  await s.sandbox.run(`my-server --claude ${s.bin}`, { env: s.env })
} finally { await s.close() }  // ends the job token, takes the AI login out, and pauses the user's sandbox
```

A program outside byoa's sandboxes, such as a harness on the user's own computer, gets a job token with no sandbox: `const t = await agents.jobToken(userId, { mcp: ['notion'] })` gives `t.token` and `t.mcp` (the proxy URLs), with the same rules as a job's token, until `t.close()`.

To move an MCP grant that the user already made elsewhere into byoa, call `agents.importMcp(userId, { name, url, oauth })` with the MCP SDK's state (`client`, `tokens`, `at`). Delete the old copy, so the grant keeps one refresh owner.

Some MCP servers have an API next to the MCP endpoint that is not MCP, such as an export. Your backend calls it with the user's grant through `agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'tasks', 'https://mcp.example.com/export')`: byoa adds the current token, refreshed by the one refresh owner, and gives you the response. By default, it sends the token only to the origin of that grant's MCP server. It does not follow redirects, and never gives you the token.

When the service's API is on another origin than its MCP server, name that origin in your own configuration, for the MCP server's origin. Only grants of that MCP server can go there, and only to that exact origin:

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  // Margins' MCP server is on margin.rippling.computer; its export is on its Convex site
  grantOrigins: { 'https://margin.rippling.computer': ['https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site'] },
})
const r = await agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'margins', 'https://helpful-tern-930.convex.site/ext/export')
```

### Your app's own tools

Give your app's own tools to `createAgents` as functions (`tools`): MCP server name → tool name → `{ description, input, run }`. `input` is the JSON Schema of the arguments. A job gets them by the server's name in `mcp`, as it gets a connected server. The harness calls them through `agents.proxy`, which checks the job token and calls `run(args, { user, job })` in your backend, for the user of that job. So you write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. What `run` returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON); when it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`: check them in `run`.

```ts
const agents = createAgents({
  ...options,
  tools: {
    todos: {
      add_todo: {
        description: 'Add one to-do.',
        input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },
        run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),
      },
      list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
    },
  },
})
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

### What the agent may do

By default (`access: 'full'`), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. This is for a sandbox that is the job's alone. An app whose agent must only use its MCP tools, such as a to-do list or a mail client, gives the job `access: 'read-only'`:

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'codex', task, mcp: ['mail'], setup: { skills }, access: 'read-only' })
```

The agent can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, so the harness can still read its skills and AGENTS.md. It cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. byoa only sets each CLI's own options: Codex runs in its own `read-only` sandbox, and Claude Code gets only its tools that read. `read-only` does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read. Use it always with `localSandbox()` on a user's own computer, where the sandbox isolates nothing.

### When the proxy is down

Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through `agents.proxy`. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (a wrong `proxyUrl`, a tunnel that ended, a firewall), the job does not start: `run` gives an `error` event with code `mcp` and ends with `ok: false`, and `session` throws `ProxyError`. A server that does not answer gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs. Without this check, a harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.

### The sandbox of a user

By default, each user has one sandbox of your app for each harness. The first job creates it. After each job, byoa pauses it (E2B pauses it; Daytona and Instabox stop it), and the next job resumes it, so files that the app wrote there and the installed harness stay. Each job gets a new job folder (`s.work`) with its own setup. One job of a user and harness runs at a time; another job waits for it (`waitMs`, default 10 minutes). When the provider no longer has the sandbox, the next job creates a new one.

An app where one user has many workspaces, such as projects or conversations, gives each job a `sandboxKey`. Each key has its own kept sandbox and its own lease, so jobs with different keys run at the same time. With the default stored login, this is true only for the fake harness: one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time. For many Codex agents of one user at the same time, each on its own machine, with one sign-in, turn on the shared login: `login: storedLogin({ parallel: true })` (see AI login below). For a new sandbox for each job, destroyed after it, set `sandboxPer: 'job'`:

```ts
agents.run(userId, { harness: 'claude', task, sandboxKey: projectId })  // one kept sandbox for each project
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, sandboxPer: 'job' })          // a new sandbox for each job; default 'user'
```

Either way, the user's AI login stays encrypted in your database, and each job gets a copy, which byoa takes out of the sandbox after the job (see AI login below). The MCP config in the sandbox points to `agents.proxy`, with a token for that one job. The real MCP tokens stay in your database. `agents.signOut` deletes the user's sandbox for that harness; when you delete a user, call `agents.deleteSandbox(userId)`, which deletes all of their sandboxes of your app at that provider, and when you delete a project, `agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey: projectId })`.

To change the provider, change `e2b(...)` to another adapter. An adapter implements one interface ([src/sandbox/types.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/src/sandbox/types.ts)): create (with volumes), resume, run a command, write a file, pause, destroy.

For Daytona, use `daytona({ apiKey })` from `byoa/sandbox/daytona` (it needs `@daytona/sdk`). Daytona allows 100 volumes per organization, so with `cliLogin` the adapter keeps every user's AI login in its own subpath of one shared volume (`byoa` by default). A sandbox mounts only that user's subpath. On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox can reach only [allowed domains](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits), so serve `agents.proxy` on one of them (for example `*.convex.site`), or use Tier 3 or higher. `*.workers.dev` is on Daytona's list but does not work: a Worker's address has two labels below it (`<worker>.<account>.workers.dev`), and Daytona does not resolve those.

For Instabox, use `instabox({ apiKey })` from `byoa/sandbox/instabox`. It calls Instabox's HTTP API itself, so it needs no package. Each sandbox starts from the `agent-browser` template (Node 22, user `user`, home `/data/home`), or from a snapshot you name (`snapshot`). byoa stops the user's sandbox after each job, so the next job starts it again with its files and no process of the last one; a sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and Instabox deletes it at the latest when the job's time is up. byoa gives a sandbox none of your account's Vault items or org Secrets, and leaves its commands out of Instabox's command history, which would otherwise keep their output (and so the AI login that byoa reads back). Instabox has no volumes, so `cliLogin` does not work there; the default stored login does. Instabox sandboxes reach every public domain, so a tunnel works for `proxyUrl`. On the free plan, a workspace has one sandbox at a time (so one user with one kept sandbox, or one job), three starts a minute (byoa waits when it gets there), and a run of 2 hours at most before Instabox pauses the sandbox.

### AI login

By default, byoa keeps each user's Claude or ChatGPT plan login in your own database, encrypted with your `encryptionKey`, through the store adapter. The sign-in is the unmodified CLI, on the lab's own page. When it ends, byoa keeps the CLI's own login files. Each job writes them into its sandbox. After the job, byoa saves them back when the CLI refreshed them, and removes them from the sandbox, also from the user's sandbox that it keeps, so your database has the only copy between jobs. One job of a user and harness holds the login at a time; another job waits for it. byoa never calls the labs' token endpoints itself. So the sandbox provider needs no volumes.

Both CLIs rotate their refresh tokens, so two sandboxes must not refresh one login. That is why one job holds it at a time. With `login: storedLogin({ parallel: true })`, the Codex jobs of one user share the login instead, each with a copy in its own sandbox (a `sandboxKey` for each, or `sandboxPer: 'job'`), and run at the same time. Codex refreshes its login 5 minutes before its access token ends, and that token lasts 10 days. byoa reads that time from the login files, and nothing else in them. When the login is due for a refresh before a job's time runs out, one job holds it alone: it waits for the user's other jobs to end, its CLI refreshes the login, byoa saves it, and the next jobs share it again. One risk stays: Codex also refreshes when OpenAI answers 401 to a token that has not run out, and two sandboxes that get that answer at the same time both refresh; one of them fails, and the user may have to sign in again. Claude Code jobs of one user always run one at a time.

The labs' published terms restrict where these tokens may be stored: Anthropic's say developers may not "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens", and OpenAI's say stored tokens must be "local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment" (see [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules)). Check them for your app.

To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so you can give them their own access rules and backups:

```ts
import { createAgents, storedLogin } from 'byoa'

// Convex: convex/schema.ts has  byoaLogin: convexTable(),  and convex/byoaLogin.ts has
//   export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions('byoaLogin')
const loginStore = convexStore(ctx, internal.byoaLogin)
// Postgres: run postgresSchema('byoa_ai_login') once
const loginStore = postgresStore({ query, table: 'byoa_ai_login' })

const agents = createAgents({ ...options, login: storedLogin({ store: loginStore, encryptionKey: loginKey }) })
```

To keep each login in a volume of that user and app instead, behind the sandbox adapter, pass `login: cliLogin` (from `byoa`). Your database then never holds the login. This needs a provider with volumes; on E2B, volumes must be turned on for your team.

### Convex

In a Convex app, byoa's state is one table and four internal functions in your deployment (`byoa/store/convex`). Call byoa from actions and HTTP actions, which can make network calls; serve `agents.proxy` from an HTTP action.

```ts
// convex/schema.ts
import { convexTable } from 'byoa/store/convex'
export default defineSchema({ ...yourTables, byoa: convexTable() })

// convex/byoa.ts
import { convexFunctions } from 'byoa/store/convex'
export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions()

// in an action or HTTP action
import { convexStore } from 'byoa/store/convex'
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa) })
```

## Test your app without a plan or a sandbox

Use `harness: 'fake'`, `localSandbox()` from `byoa/sandbox/local` and `memoryStore()`. The fake harness runs no model. It calls MCP tools through the real proxy: each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one call.

To test byoa itself: `npm test` (V10, V12, the fake-harness tests and the unit tests), and `npm run test:v11` (V11; it downloads about 600 MB). CI runs both on every commit. With `DAYTONA_API_KEY` set, `npm test` also checks the Daytona adapter against Daytona (with `BYOA_DAYTONA_VOLUMES=1` too, also its volumes; that needs a key with the volume permissions); with `E2B_API_KEY` too, it runs V4 ([test/v4.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/v4.test.ts)), which needs `cloudflared` to give the proxy a public URL. On a Daytona org on Tier 1 or 2, also set `BYOA_V4_RELAY` to a relay on an allowed domain, such as [test/relay](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/test/relay/convex/http.ts) deployed to a temporary Convex project. `npm run test:e2b` checks the E2B adapter against E2B and runs V8 there (a user's jobs in one paused and resumed sandbox, and `sandboxPer: 'job'`); it needs `E2B_API_KEY`, and with `BYOA_E2B_VOLUMES=1` also checks volumes, for an E2B team with volumes turned on. `npm run test:instabox` does the same on Instabox; it needs `INSTABOX_API_KEY`. `BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox` runs V4 on E2B and Instabox.

## Example app

[examples/todo](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo) is an AI-native to-do list on byoa: the user signs in with their own plan, connects their to-dos one time, and asks Claude Code or Codex to change them. Its backend uses byoa in 35 lines. Its tests use the fake harness, and CI runs them on every commit.

## How we will verify it

We call version 1 done only when all of these checks pass. The full list is in [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification).

1. **Two apps use it.** An existing app moves its own login, connector and sandbox code to byoa. A second app uses byoa with no copied code.
2. **Two harnesses work.** One user runs the same task with Claude Code and with Codex, each on that user's own plan.
3. **Two providers work.** The same user, with the same MCP grants and skills, runs a job on E2B and then on Daytona or Instabox. Only the adapter changes.
4. **Tokens stay out of the sandbox.** A test searches the sandbox's environment, files and process list for each real MCP token after a job. It must find none.
5. **One refresh owner.** Two jobs run at the same time (one sandbox for each job) and both need a token refresh. The provider sees one refresh request, and no grant is revoked.
6. **The sandbox lifecycle works.** By default, a user's next job resumes the sandbox that was paused after the last one; when the provider lost it, the next job gets a new one. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, the library destroys the sandbox after a job. In neither case does the user sign in to an MCP server again.

## Rules we follow

- We run the real, unmodified `claude` and `codex` binaries. We never pretend to be another client.
- The user signs in through Anthropic's or OpenAI's own sign-in page.
- One app's AI login is used only by that app.
- The labs' terms restrict where an AI login may be stored. byoa keeps it in your database by default, so each app checks those terms and signs its own agreements with the labs. See [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules).

## License

Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/LICENSE).

Image: Bring your own agent.

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md

# byoa requirements, version 1

**Status:** draft, 2026-11-22. **Owner:** Ian Hsiao.

This document says what version 1 of byoa must do and how we check it. It does not say how to build it. "MUST" and "SHOULD" have their usual meanings (RFC 2119).

## Goal

A developer makes an app AI-native in one day, not in weeks. The app runs the user's own Claude Code or Codex in any sandbox. The user signs in to ChatGPT or Claude one time and connects each MCP tool one time.

## Users of this library

- **App developer.** Imports byoa into their own backend. Does not want to build login, MCP OAuth, skills loading, harness updates or sandbox code.
- **End user.** Uses the developer's app. Has a ChatGPT or Claude plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion, Gmail or Heptabase.

## Scope

In scope for version 1:

- Harnesses: Claude Code and Codex. Both from the first version.
- Sandbox providers: E2B, Daytona and Instabox.
- Backends: Node, and Convex actions. Cloudflare Workers SHOULD work if it costs little.
- Store adapters: Convex and Postgres.

Out of scope for version 1:

- A hosted service. byoa never runs a server for other apps.
- Sharing one user's AI login between different apps.
- Harnesses other than Claude Code and Codex (OpenCode, Amp, Pi, Cursor).
- A UI kit. The library gives data and events; the app draws its own UI.

## Requirements

### R1. AI login

- **R1.1** byoa MUST sign the user in to Claude Code by running the unmodified `claude` CLI login in the sandbox. The user completes sign-in on Anthropic's own page.
- **R1.2** byoa MUST sign the user in to Codex by running the unmodified `codex login --device-auth` in the sandbox. The user enters the code on OpenAI's own page.
- **R1.3** byoa MUST give the app the sign-in URL and code as data, so the app can show them on any device (for example a phone).
- **R1.4** By default, byoa MUST keep the login (the CLI's own login files) in the app's own database, through the store adapter (R6), encrypted with a key that the app gives, for one user of one app. Each job MUST get a copy in its sandbox. After the job, byoa MUST save the files back when the CLI changed them (a token refresh), and MUST remove them from the sandbox, also from a sandbox that it keeps for the user's next job (R5.4). So between jobs the store is the only copy. By default, byoa MUST NOT let two sandboxes hold one user's login at the same time, so that two token refreshes do not revoke each other. The app MAY turn on a shared login for Codex (`parallel`), so that one user's jobs run at the same time: while the login is not due for a refresh before a job's time runs out, the jobs of one user each hold a copy; when it is due, one job MUST hold it alone, after the other jobs end. To know when a login is due, byoa MAY read the time its access token ends from the login files. byoa MUST NOT use a token, and MUST NOT call the lab's token endpoints itself; the CLI is the only client that uses the tokens.
- **R1.5** The login part MUST be replaceable, with no change to R2 to R5. byoa MUST also ship a login that stays in a volume of that one user of that one app, mounted through the sandbox adapter (R5.3), which the app's database never holds.
- **R1.6** byoa MUST report login state: `signed-in`, `signed-out`, `expired`.

### R2. MCP connections

- **R2.1** byoa MUST connect a remote MCP server for one user with MCP authorization (OAuth 2.1 with PKCE). It MUST use Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them, and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not.
- **R2.2** byoa MUST also accept a bearer token that the user pastes.
- **R2.3** Each grant MUST have exactly one refresh owner: the app's backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time MUST cause one refresh request.
- **R2.4** byoa MUST store grants through the store adapter (R6), in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives.
- **R2.5** byoa MUST let the app choose which MCP servers each job gets. (Bookish gives MCP servers only to jobs that the user asked for.)
- **R2.6** byoa MUST let the app's backend send a request with a user's grant to an API of the same service that is not MCP (for example an export). By default, the token goes only to the origin of the grant's MCP server. The app's backend MAY name more origins for the grants of one MCP server origin, as exact origins (https, no path, no wildcard), in its own configuration; the MCP server, the sandbox and the user MUST NOT be able to add one. byoa MUST add the token only for those origins, MUST NOT follow redirects, and MUST NOT give the token to the app. (Margins' MCP server is on `margin.rippling.computer`, and its export is on `helpful-tern-930.convex.site`.)
- **R2.7** byoa MUST let the app give its own tools as functions in its backend. The proxy (R3) MUST serve them as the tools of an MCP server, only to a job that the app gave them (R2.5), and MUST give each call the user of the job. The app writes no MCP server, and no user connects anything for them.

### R3. MCP proxy: real tokens stay outside the sandbox

- **R3.1** The `mcp.json` in the sandbox MUST point to the app's proxy, with a short-lived token for one job and one user.
- **R3.2** The proxy MUST add the real token to each request and send it to the MCP server.
- **R3.3** No real MCP token MUST be in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time.
- **R3.4** The proxy MUST refuse a job token after the job ends.
- **R3.5** Before the harness starts, byoa MUST check from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through the proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy, the job MUST NOT start, and MUST end with an error. A server that does not answer MUST give an error event. (A harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.)

### R4. Skills, AGENTS.md and config

- **R4.1** byoa MUST write skills in the Agent Skills format where each harness reads them (for example `.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`).
- **R4.2** byoa MUST write AGENTS.md, and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, from one source.
- **R4.3** byoa MUST write MCP config in each harness's own format: JSON for Claude Code, TOML for Codex.
- **R4.4** byoa SHOULD read an Agent Plugins 1.0 package (`plugin.json`, `skills/`, `mcp.json`).

### R5. Harness and sandbox

- **R5.1** byoa MUST install a pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, or use a provider template with that version.
- **R5.2** A new harness version MUST reach every user at their next job. (Bookish had to copy a new core into old sandboxes, because a template reaches only new sandboxes.)
- **R5.3** Each sandbox provider MUST be one adapter with one interface: create, resume, run a command, write a file, mount a volume, pause, destroy. A provider with no volumes (Instabox) refuses a volume, so the volume login of R1.5 does not work on it; the stored login of R1.4 does.
- **R5.4** The lifecycle MUST be the app's choice, with the same app code on every provider:
  - **One kept sandbox per user (the default).** Each user has one sandbox of the app for each harness. The first job creates it. After each job, byoa pauses it (E2B: pause; Daytona and Instabox: stop), and the next job resumes it, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness runs at a time; another job waits. When the provider no longer has the sandbox (it was deleted, or it expired), the next job creates a new one. A sandbox that times out during a job (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not deleted, and no process of that job runs when it resumes. byoa MUST delete the user's sandbox at sign-out, and MUST give the app a way to delete it, such as when it deletes the user.
  - **Many kept sandboxes per user (a `sandboxKey` for each job).** The same, but each key that the app gives a job (such as a project or a conversation) has its own sandbox and its own lease, so jobs with different keys run at the same time. With the stored login of R1.4, jobs that need the same AI login still run one at a time, unless the app turned on the shared login for Codex. The app MUST be able to delete the sandbox of one key, or all of the user's.
  - **One sandbox per job (`sandboxPer: 'job'`).** Create a sandbox, load the user's setup, run the job, destroy the sandbox.

  In all three, the user's AI login (R1.4) and grants (R2) stay in the app's database, and the security properties of R1.4 and R3 do not depend on the choice: no real MCP token goes into the sandbox, a job token is refused after its job, and no copy of the AI login stays in the sandbox between jobs.
- **R5.5** `agents.run` MUST stream events (text, tool calls, permission requests, errors, end) in one schema for both harnesses.
- **R5.6** byoa MUST let the app limit what the agent of a job may do, with each CLI's own options only (Lab rules). With `access: 'read-only'`, the agent MUST be able to call the job's MCP tools and to read files, so that the harness can read its skills and AGENTS.md; it MUST NOT be able to change a file, or to reach the network by itself. The default (`full`) is every tool of the harness with no approval, for a sandbox that is the job's alone.

### R6. Store adapter

- **R6.1** The store adapter MUST be a small interface (get, put, delete, compare-and-set) that an app can write for its own database.
- **R6.2** Compare-and-set is needed for R2.3.

### R7. Developer experience

- **R7.1** A new app MUST reach its first agent run in under 50 lines of its own code.
- **R7.2** byoa MUST include a fake harness for tests, so apps can test without a plan or a sandbox.
- **R7.3** byoa SHOULD ship an agent skill in the Agent Skills format (`skills/byoa/`) that teaches a coding agent to add byoa to an app, and its site SHOULD serve the docs for LLMs as `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. Both MUST name only the API that byoa has.

## Lab rules

byoa follows the labs' published rules as read on 2026-11-22:

- Anthropic ([legal and compliance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance)) allows an end user to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own plan, including where a platform hosts Claude Code. It forbids third parties to "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens", unless Anthropic agrees otherwise.
- OpenAI ([Sign in with ChatGPT Terms](https://openai.com/policies/sign-in-with-chatgpt-terms/), effective 2026-11-04) requires that "any persistent storage of Authentication Tokens must be local and under the user's control, not in a remote or managed environment", and that the plan is used "only for the application they connected". Paid or remotely hosted apps must [apply](https://openai.com/form/sign-in-with-chatgpt-interest/) to be partners.

So byoa MUST:

- run only unmodified `claude` and `codex` binaries, and never pretend to be another client;
- send the user to the lab's own sign-in page;
- not share one AI login between apps.

The labs' terms above restrict where these tokens may be stored. byoa keeps the AI login in the app's database by default (R1.4), and ships a per-user volume as an option (R1.5). Each app checks the labs' terms for its own use.

Each app is responsible for its own agreements with the labs. We plan to sign agreements for our own apps when they have traction.

## Verification

Version 1 is done when every check below passes. Each check names the requirement it proves.

| # | Check | How | Proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | Bookish uses byoa | Replace `site/agent/login.ts`, `site/agent/sandbox.ts` and `src/core/connectors.ts` in Bookish with byoa. Bookish's existing e2e tests pass. | R1, R2, R5 |
| V2 | A second app uses byoa | A second app (the to-do example in `examples/todo`, Margins, or the mail app) runs its first agent job with byoa, on a real sandbox provider and a real plan, with no code copied from Bookish. Count the app's own lines. | R7.1 |
| V3 | Both harnesses | One test user runs the same task with Claude Code and with Codex. Both runs use that user's own plan. | R1.1, R1.2, R5.5 |
| V4 | Two providers | The same user runs a job on E2B, then on Daytona or Instabox. The second job uses the same MCP grants and skills with no new MCP sign-in. | R5.3, R2 |
| V5 | Tokens stay out | After a job with an MCP call, a test searches the sandbox's environment, every file, and `/proc/*/cmdline` and `/proc/*/environ` for each real token. It finds none. | R3.3 |
| V6 | Old job tokens fail | A job token is used after its job ends. The proxy refuses it. | R3.4 |
| V7 | One refresh | Two jobs start at the same time with an expired access token (with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, so that they run at the same time). The MCP server's token endpoint gets one refresh request, and both jobs succeed. | R2.3, R6.2 |
| V8 | Sandbox lifecycle | By default, a user's second job runs in the first job's sandbox, which was paused between them, and jobs with two sandbox keys run in two more sandboxes, of which deleting one key removes only that one. When the provider no longer has a sandbox, the next job works in a new one with no new sign-in, and deleting the user's sandbox removes it at the provider. With `sandboxPer: 'job'`, after a job its sandbox no longer exists at the provider. | R5.4 |
| V9 | Harness update | Change the pinned Claude Code version. The next job for an existing user runs the new version. | R5.2 |
| V10 | Config formats | For a sample plugin, the files byoa writes match the expected files for each harness, byte for byte. | R4 |
| V11 | Unmodified binaries | The test checks the hash of the installed `claude` and `codex` binaries against the published packages. | Lab rules |
| V12 | The docs match the API | A test checks that every `agents.*` method, and every name imported from byoa, in the README and the agent skill exists in byoa. | R7.3 |
| V13 | The app's own tools | A job with a real harness calls a tool that the app gave as a function. The function runs in the backend for the job's user. The app has no MCP server, and the user has no grant. | R2.7 |
| V14 | A proxy that is down | A job starts while its sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The harness does not start, and the job ends with an `mcp` error and `ok: false`. | R3.5 |
| V15 | Read-only access | A job with a real harness and `access: 'read-only'` reads its skill and calls an MCP tool. A command that writes a file fails, and a command that opens a network connection fails. | R5.6 |
| V16 | Jobs at the same time | With the shared login turned on, one user starts three Codex jobs with three sandbox keys. They run at the same time with one sign-in, and the login works after them. | R1.4, R5.4 |

V1 to V9 and V13 to V16 run against real providers and real plans, so they cost money. They run before each release, not on every commit. V10, V11, V12 and the fake-harness tests run on every commit; these include V13, V14 and V16 with the fake harness and a stand-in CLI. In this repository: `npm test` runs V10, V12 and the fake-harness tests, `npm run test:v11` runs V11, and the job `example-todo` runs the to-do example's fake-harness tests (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). With `E2B_API_KEY` and `DAYTONA_API_KEY` set, `npm test` also runs V4 (`test/v4.test.ts`); `BYOA_V4_PROVIDERS=e2b,instabox` runs it on E2B and Instabox. `npm run test:e2b` runs V8 on E2B (`test/e2b.test.ts`), with `DAYTONA_API_KEY` set `npm test` runs V8 on Daytona (`test/daytona.test.ts`), and `npm run test:instabox` runs V8 on Instabox (`test/instabox.test.ts`). On an Instabox plan that allows fewer than three sandboxes (the free plan allows one), V8 there checks one sandbox key alone, not two at the same time.

## Open questions

- Does the first version support Cloudflare Workers, or only Node and Convex?
- How does a Claude login move from one sandbox provider to another without the app holding it? Today the user signs in again.
- Do Anthropic and OpenAI accept the default stored login (R1.4) for apps that run their unmodified CLIs, or does an app need an agreement with them? We will ask them.
- Does the shared login (R1.4) become the default? Codex also refreshes its login when OpenAI answers 401 to a token that has not run out. Two sandboxes that get that answer at the same time both refresh, and one refresh fails. We do not know how often that occurs, or when Claude Code refreshes.
- `access: 'read-only'` (R5.6) does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read, also the CLI's own login files. Does byoa need a level that lets the agent read only its job folder, for apps that run on the user's own computer?
- How long does a user's paused sandbox stay? Today byoa deletes it only at sign-out and when the app calls `deleteSandbox`. E2B and Instabox keep a paused or stopped sandbox with no time limit; Daytona archives a stopped one after 7 days, and the next job restores it more slowly. Does byoa need a limit for users who stop using an app?
- Do we write a spec for credential references as an extension of Agent Plugins, and send it to the Agentic AI Foundation?

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa/SKILL.md

---
name: byoa
description: Adds byoa to an app, so the app runs each user's own Claude Code or Codex in a sandbox (E2B, Daytona, Instabox or local), on the user's own Claude or ChatGPT plan, with the user's MCP connections. Use when you add AI agent jobs to an app's backend with byoa, write its sign-in, MCP connect, proxy or callback routes, stream agents.run events to a UI, write a byoa store adapter, or test with byoa's fake harness.
---

# Add byoa to an app

byoa is a library. It runs inside the app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex actions). It is not a hosted service. The app gives it a sandbox adapter and a store adapter. byoa then signs each user in to their own plan, keeps their MCP grants, and runs each job in that user's sandbox (or, as an option, a new sandbox for each job).

The reference app is the to-do example: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/tree/main/examples/todo. Its `app.ts` holds all of its byoa code. Read it before you write the app's code, and copy its patterns. One pattern is older than byoa's `tools` option: the example runs its own MCP server for its to-dos and connects it for each user with a bearer token. In a new app, give the app's own tools to `createAgents` as `tools` (section 5).

The full API, with every option and event, is in [reference/api.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa/reference/api.md). The rules every app must follow are in "Lab rules" below. Do not skip them.

## 1. Install

byoa is not on npm yet. Install it from GitHub:

```sh
npm install github:madeyexz/byoa     # npm builds it on install
bun add github:madeyexz/byoa        # Bun loads its TypeScript source
```

Also install the sandbox SDK that the app uses: `e2b` for E2B, `@daytona/sdk` for Daytona; Instabox needs none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. Do not write `npm install byoa`: that package is not byoa until version 1.

## 2. One createAgents

Make one `agents` object in the backend. Do it once per process (or once per Convex action).

```ts
import { createAgents } from 'byoa'
import { e2b } from 'byoa/sandbox/e2b'              // or: daytona from 'byoa/sandbox/daytona', instabox from 'byoa/sandbox/instabox'
import { postgresStore } from 'byoa/store/postgres' // or: convexStore, or the app's own Store

const agents = createAgents({
  app: 'myapp',                                     // lower-case letters, digits, -; at most 24
  sandbox: e2b({ apiKey: process.env.E2B_API_KEY }),
  store: postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }),
  encryptionKey: process.env.BYOA_KEY!,             // openssl rand -base64 32; keep it the same between restarts
  proxyUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/mcp',   // public HTTPS; serve agents.proxy here and below
  oauth: { redirectUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/byoa/callback' },
  tools: { todos: todoTools },                      // the app's own tools, as functions: see section 5
})
```

- **Store.** `postgresStore` needs its table once: run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` (from `byoa/store/postgres`). For Convex, see reference/api.md. For another database, write a `Store` with four methods: `get`, `put`, `delete`, `cas` (compare-and-set). The example's `sqliteStore` in `examples/todo/todos.ts` is one in 19 lines. A new version on every write is required, and a deleted and rewritten key must never get an old version back.
- **Sandbox.** `e2b()`, `daytona()` and `instabox()` read their API key from `E2B_API_KEY` / `DAYTONA_API_KEY` / `INSTABOX_API_KEY` when you give none. Instabox has no volumes, so use the default `storedLogin()` there, not `cliLogin`. The default E2B template is named `byoa`, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with `404: template 'byoa' not found`. Build it one time with `buildE2BTemplate()` from `byoa/sandbox/e2b`, or pass `e2b({ template: 'base' })`: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds). `localSandbox()` from `byoa/sandbox/local` is a folder on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests.
- **The sandbox must reach `proxyUrl`.** With E2B, Daytona or Instabox it must be a public HTTPS URL (in development, a tunnel such as `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000`). On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, only allowed domains work, such as `*.convex.site` or `*.workers.dev`.

## 3. Routes the app must serve

The app serves two byoa routes, and its own API routes that call `agents.*`. All handlers are fetch handlers (`Request` → `Response`). On Node, wrap the app's handler with `toNodeListener` from `byoa/node`.

```ts
if (url.pathname.startsWith('/byoa/mcp/')) return agents.proxy(req)  // the MCP proxy: no app session check here
if (url.pathname === '/byoa/callback') {                               // the MCP server's sign-in page sends the browser here
  const p = url.searchParams
  await agents.finishMcp({ state: p.get('state') ?? '', code: p.get('code') ?? undefined, error: p.get('error') ?? undefined })
  return Response.redirect(`${publicUrl}/`, 302)
}
```

- The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put the app's own sign-in check in front of it, because the harness in the sandbox has no app session.
- `finishMcp` returns `{ user, name }`. It finds the user from the stored `state`, so the callback needs no session either.
- Every other route reads the user from the app's own session. The `userId` you pass to byoa is the app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls (the example's `x-user` header is a stand-in only).

## 4. Sign the user in to their plan

The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives the app only that page's URL (and, for Codex, a code).

```ts
// Claude: show the URL; the user signs in and pastes the code that Anthropic's page shows
const { url } = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'claude')
const r = await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'claude', { code })            // r.state: 'signed-in' or an error

// ChatGPT (Codex): show the URL and the code; the user enters the code on OpenAI's page
const { url, code } = await agents.connectLogin(userId, 'codex')
const r = await agents.finishLogin(userId, 'codex', { waitMs: 20_000 })  // call again while r.state === 'pending'

await agents.loginState(userId, 'claude')  // 'signed-in' | 'signed-out' | 'expired'
await agents.signOut(userId, 'claude')
```

Show `url` as a link or a QR code, so the user can sign in on another device. Keep each request short (for example `waitMs: 20_000`) and let the page call `finishLogin` again while the state is `pending`. This also works from short-lived backends such as Convex actions.

**Where the login stays.** With no `login` option, byoa keeps the CLI's own login files encrypted in the app's store (`storedLogin()`, the default). Each job gets a copy in its sandbox; after the job, byoa saves it back when the CLI refreshed it and removes it from the sandbox. One job of a user and harness holds the login at a time. Options:

- `login: storedLogin({ store: loginStore, encryptionKey: loginKey })`: a table and a key of their own.
- `login: cliLogin`: a volume of that user, behind the sandbox adapter. The app's database never holds the login. It needs a provider with volumes (E2B volumes must be turned on for the team).

Tell the developer that the labs' terms restrict where these tokens may be stored (see Lab rules), and let them choose. Do not choose for them in silence.

## 5. Connect MCP tools, one time per user

```ts
// A server with its own sign-in (MCP authorization, OAuth 2.1 with PKCE)
const c = await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://mcp.notion.com/mcp', { name: 'notion' })
if (!c.connected) return Response.json({ signInUrl: c.signInUrl })  // send the browser there; it comes back to /byoa/callback

// A server that takes a token the user pasted (or the app's own server, with this user's token)
await agents.connectMcp(userId, 'https://myapp.example.com/mcp', { name: 'todos', bearer: token })

await agents.listMcp(userId)            // [{ name, url }]
await agents.removeMcp(userId, 'notion')
```

- `name`: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. The job asks for servers by this name.
- The URL must be `https://` (or `http://` on localhost). With `bearer`, byoa checks the token with one MCP `initialize` and throws if the server refuses it.
- A sign-in that is not finished in 15 minutes runs out; call `connectMcp` again.
- byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner. Do not refresh or read the tokens in app code. To call a non-MCP API of the same service (for example an export), use `agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, name, url)`.

**The app's own tools.** Do not write an MCP server for the app's own data. Give the tools to `createAgents` as functions, and name the group in the job's `mcp`:

```ts
const todoTools = {
  add_todo: {
    description: 'Add one to-do.',
    input: { type: 'object', properties: { title: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['title'] },  // JSON Schema of the arguments
    run: ({ title }, { user }) => db.addTodo(user, String(title)),                             // in the backend, for the job's user
  },
  list_todos: { description: "List the user's to-dos.", run: (_args, { user }) => db.todos(user) },
}
const agents = createAgents({ ...options, tools: { todos: todoTools } })
agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp: ['todos'] })
```

- `agents.proxy` serves them at `<proxyUrl>/todos` and checks the job token. `user` is the user of the job; never take the user from the arguments.
- What `run` returns goes to the agent: a string as it is, other values as JSON. When it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`: check them in `run`.
- No user connects anything for them, and `listMcp` does not list them. `connectMcp` refuses their names.

## 6. Run a job and stream its events

```ts
for await (const ev of agents.run(userId, {
  harness: 'claude',                   // 'claude' | 'codex' | 'fake'
  task,                                // the user's request
  mcp: ['notion'],                     // the servers this job gets; default none
  setup: { agentsMd, skills },         // AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code); skills: [{ name, files: { 'SKILL.md': '...' } }]
  access: 'read-only',                 // what the agent may do; default 'full'
})) {
  // ev.type: 'start' | 'text' | 'tool_call' | 'tool_result' | 'permission' | 'error' | 'end'
}
```

- The events are the same for Claude Code and Codex. The full schema is in reference/api.md.
- `run` never throws for job failures. It yields `error` events (`code`: `signed-out`, `expired`, `harness`, `sandbox` or `mcp`) and always ends with one `end` event (`ok`, `result`, `usage`). On `signed-out` or `expired`, show the sign-in again.
- A server in `mcp` that the user has not connected gives an `error` with code `mcp`, and the job runs without it.
- **The proxy check.** Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the sandbox that each of the job's servers answers through the proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy, the job does not start: an `error` with code `mcp`, then `end` with `ok: false` (`session` throws `ProxyError`). A server that does not answer gives an `error` with code `mcp`, and the job runs. Show these errors: they mean a wrong `proxyUrl`, a tunnel that ended, or a server that is down.
- **What the agent may do (`access`).** With `'full'` (the default), the agent has every tool of its harness with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. That is for coding agents in a sandbox that is the job's alone. With `'read-only'`, the agent calls the job's MCP tools and reads files (the harness reads its skills this way: do not forbid the shell in AGENTS.md, because Codex reads a skill with `cat`); it cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. Use `'read-only'` when the agent needs only its MCP tools (a to-do list, a mail client), and always with `localSandbox()` on a user's own computer. It does not hide files: the agent can read each file its user can read. Ask the developer which one each kind of job needs.
- **The sandbox.** By default (`sandboxPer: 'user'`), each user has one sandbox of the app for each harness: the first job creates it, byoa pauses it after each job and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness runs at a time; another waits up to `waitMs` (default 10 minutes; set it shorter on short-lived backends such as Convex actions). A sandbox the provider lost is replaced by a new one. When one user has many workspaces (projects, conversations), pass `sandboxKey` in `run` or `session`: each key gets its own kept sandbox and lease. `sandboxPer: 'job'` gives each job a new sandbox and destroys it after the job; use it when nothing may stay between jobs. With the default stored login, a user's Claude Code or Codex jobs run one after the other in every mode, also with different sandbox keys: one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time, and another waits for it. For many Codex agents of one user at the same time (a fleet), pass `login: storedLogin({ parallel: true })` and give each agent a `sandboxKey`: the jobs then share the login while it is not due for a refresh. Tell the developer the risk that stays (reference/api.md, `storedLogin`), and let them choose. Ask the developer which they want.
- `agents.signOut` deletes the user's sandbox for that harness. When the app deletes a user, call `agents.deleteSandbox(userId)` too; when it deletes a project that had a key, `agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey })`.
- If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call `return()` on the generator): byoa then closes the job token and pauses (or destroys) the sandbox. The example's `ndjson()` in `app.ts` streams the events as JSON lines and does this on `cancel`.
- To run the app's own program around the unmodified harness, use `agents.session(userId, { harness, mcp })` and call `s.close()` in a `finally`. See reference/api.md.

## 7. Test without a plan or a sandbox

Use `harness: 'fake'`, `localSandbox()` from `byoa/sandbox/local` and `memoryStore()` from `byoa`. The fake harness runs no model. Each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json>` is one MCP call through the real proxy, so a test proves the app's routes, grants and proxy end to end. With the local sandbox, `proxyUrl` can be `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp`. Copy `examples/todo/todo.test.ts`. Do not offer `fake` to end users in production.

## Lab rules

Every app on byoa must follow these rules. If a request breaks one, stop and tell the developer.

- Run only the unmodified `claude` and `codex` binaries that byoa installs (pinned, and checked in byoa's own tests). Do not patch them, wrap them to change what they send, or set headers or a user agent to pretend to be another client.
- Send the user to the lab's own sign-in page, from `connectLogin`. Do not embed, proxy or copy that page, and never ask the user for a password or an API key in place of it.
- Never read, export or call the labs' APIs with the user's AI tokens. The CLI is the only client that uses them. Do not call the labs' token endpoints.
- One app's AI login is only for that app. Give each app its own `app` name and its own store. Never share a login between apps.
- Real MCP tokens never go into the sandbox. Give a job its servers with `mcp: [...]`. Never put a grant's token in `setup`, the task, environment variables or files.
- The labs' terms restrict where AI logins may be stored. Anthropic says third parties may not "collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens" without its agreement. OpenAI says stored tokens must be "local and under the user's control", and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. byoa's default keeps the login in the app's database; `cliLogin` keeps it in a per-user volume. Each app checks the terms and makes its own agreements: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#lab-rules

## Check your work

- The app's byoa code is small: the example's backend uses byoa in 35 lines. If you write sign-in, OAuth, token refresh or sandbox code yourself, you are rebuilding byoa: use its API.
- Run the app's tests with the fake harness and the local sandbox.
- Every API name you use is in reference/api.md. If a name is not there, read the source (`src/agents.ts` in https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa) before you use it. The API can change before version 1.

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/skills/byoa/reference/api.md

# byoa API reference

This is the API in https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa today (version 0.1, before version 1). It can change before version 1. The source of truth is `src/agents.ts`, `src/index.ts` and the files they import.

## Imports

| Import | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `byoa` | `createAgents`, `LoginError`, `ProxyError`, `SandboxGoneError`, `memoryStore`, `storedLogin`, `cliLogin`, `harnessFiles`, `readPlugin`, `JOB_TOKEN_ENV`, `PINS`, `PACKAGES`, `ensureHarness`, `LOGIN_FILES`, `clientMetadataDocument`; types `AgentsOptions`, `RunOptions`, `RunHarness`, `ConnectResult`, `Session`, `SessionOptions`, `JobToken`, `Store`, `Entry`, `Sandbox`, `SandboxProvider`, `AgentEvent`, `Usage`, `AppTools`, `AppTool`, `Access`, `Setup`, `Skill`, `Plugin`, `LoginState`, `LoginStart`, `LoginResult` |
| `byoa/sandbox/e2b` | `e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? })`, `buildE2BTemplate(name?, { apiKey?, pins? })`, `e2bTemplate(pins?)`. Needs the `e2b` package. |
| `byoa/sandbox/daytona` | `daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? })`. Needs `@daytona/sdk`. |
| `byoa/sandbox/instabox` | `instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? })`. Needs no package. No volumes: use `storedLogin()`, not `cliLogin`. |
| `byoa/sandbox/local` | `localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? })`: folders on this computer, for tests and development only. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux. |
| `byoa/store/postgres` | `postgresStore({ query, table? })`, `postgresSchema(table?)`, `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` |
| `byoa/store/convex` | `convexTable()`, `convexFunctions(table?)`, `convexStore(ctx, fns)`. Needs `convex`. |
| `byoa/node` | `toNodeListener(handler)` (a fetch handler as a `node:http` listener), `readPluginDir(dir)` |
| `byoa/verify` | `verifyHarness(sandbox, harness, bin, pins?)`: checks the installed binary against the published npm package |

## createAgents(options)

```ts
interface AgentsOptions {
  app: string                 // lower-case letters, digits, -; at most 24. Names the app's sandboxes and login volumes.
  sandbox: SandboxProvider
  store: Store
  encryptionKey: string       // 32 random bytes as base64. Encrypts MCP grants and, by default, AI logins.
  proxyUrl: string            // public URL where the app serves agents.proxy; each server is at <proxyUrl>/<name>
  oauth: { redirectUrl: string; clientMetadataUrl?: string; clientName?: string }
  pins?: { claude: string; codex: string }   // default PINS
  login?: (deps) => LoginDriver              // default storedLogin(); or cliLogin
  jobTimeoutMs?: number                      // default 30 minutes
  sandboxPer?: 'user' | 'job'                // default 'user': kept sandboxes, paused between jobs
  waitMs?: number                            // sandboxPer 'user': how long a job waits for another job of its sandbox; default 10 minutes
  grantOrigins?: Record<string, string[]>    // more exact origins for fetchWithGrant, by MCP server origin
  tools?: AppTools                           // the app's own tools: MCP server name → tool name → { description?, input?, run }
}
```

- `oauth.redirectUrl`: the app's route that calls `finishMcp`.
- `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`: an HTTPS URL where the app serves `agents.clientMetadata()` (a Client ID Metadata Document). Without it, byoa uses only Dynamic Client Registration.
- `oauth.clientName`: the name the MCP server shows on its consent page. Default: `app`.
- `sandboxPer`: `'user'` (the default): the first job of a user and harness creates the user's sandbox; byoa pauses it after each job (E2B pause, Daytona and Instabox stop) and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness at a time. A job's `sandboxKey` (in `run` and `session`) gives the user one kept sandbox, with its own lease, for each key. A sandbox the provider no longer has is replaced by a new one. `'job'`: a new sandbox for each job, destroyed after it. With the default `storedLogin()`, one job of a user and harness holds the AI login at a time, so the user's Claude Code or Codex jobs run one after the other in both modes, also with different sandbox keys; `storedLogin({ parallel: true })` lets a user's Codex jobs run at the same time.

- `tools`: the app's own tools, as functions in the backend. `{ todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } }` is an MCP server `todos` with one tool. `input`: the JSON Schema of the arguments (an object schema; default: no arguments). `run(args, { user, job })` runs for the user of the job; what it returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON), and what it throws goes to the agent as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against `input`. A job gets the server by its name in `mcp`; the proxy serves it at `<proxyUrl>/<name>`. Server names: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32; tool names: letters, digits, _ and -, at most 64. `listMcp` does not list them, and `connectMcp` refuses their names.

It returns an object with the methods below.

## AI login

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `connectLogin(user, 'claude' \| 'codex')` | `{ harness, url, code? }`. `url`: the lab's own sign-in page. `code`: Codex only, the code to enter on OpenAI's page. |
| `finishLogin(user, h, { code?, waitMs? })` | `{ state: 'signed-in' \| 'signed-out' \| 'expired' \| 'pending', error? }`. Claude: pass `code` (the code Anthropic's page shows). Codex: no code; `waitMs` waits that long; call again while `pending`. |
| `loginState(user, h)` | `'signed-in' \| 'signed-out' \| 'expired'` |
| `signOut(user, h)` | `void`. Also deletes the user's sandbox for `h`. |
| `deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? }?)` | `void`. Deletes the user's kept sandboxes of this app at this provider: all of them (when the app deletes the user), or those of one harness or one sandbox key (when it deletes a project). The login and grants stay. |

Login drivers:

- `storedLogin({ store?, encryptionKey?, waitMs?, parallel? })` (default): the CLI's own login files, encrypted in the store. `store` and `encryptionKey` default to the app's. One job of a user and harness holds the login at a time, and another waits for it. `waitMs`: how long a job waits for the login (default 10 minutes). `parallel: true`: the Codex jobs of one user share the login, each with a copy in its own sandbox, while Codex will not refresh it before the job's time runs out (byoa reads the time the access token ends from the login files: Codex refreshes 5 minutes before it, and its token lasts 10 days). When it is due for a refresh, one job holds it alone: it waits for the other jobs, and the jobs after it wait for it. The risk that stays: Codex also refreshes when OpenAI answers 401 to a token that has not run out; two sandboxes that get that answer at the same time both refresh, one fails, and the user may have to sign in again. Claude Code jobs always run one at a time.
- `cliLogin`: the login stays in a volume of the user, mounted through the sandbox adapter. Needs a provider with volumes.

## MCP connections

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `connectMcp(user, url, { name, bearer? })` | `{ name, connected: true }` or `{ name, connected: false, signInUrl }`. Send the browser to `signInUrl`. |
| `finishMcp({ state, code?, error? })` | `{ user, name }`. Call it in the `oauth.redirectUrl` route with the query parameters. |
| `listMcp(user)` | `[{ name, url }]` |
| `removeMcp(user, name)` | `void` |
| `importMcp(user, { name, url, oauth })` | `{ name }`. Moves a grant made elsewhere into byoa; `oauth` is the MCP SDK's state (`client`, `tokens`, `at`). Delete the old copy, so the grant keeps one refresh owner. |
| `fetchWithGrant(user, name, url, init?)` | `Response`. A request with the grant's current token, only to the origin of the grant's MCP server (and `grantOrigins` for it). No redirects. The app never gets the token. |
| `clientMetadata()` | The Client ID Metadata Document to serve at `oauth.clientMetadataUrl`. |

`name`: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. `url`: `https://`, or `http://` on localhost.

## The proxy

`agents.proxy` is a fetch handler (`Request` → `Response`). Serve it at `proxyUrl` and every path below it (`<proxyUrl>/<name>`). It checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request to the MCP server; for the app's own `tools`, it calls the tool's `run`. It refuses a job token after the job ends. Do not put the app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header `x-byoa-proxy: 1`.

## Jobs

### run(user, options): AsyncGenerator<AgentEvent>

```ts
interface RunOptions {
  harness: 'claude' | 'codex' | 'fake'
  task: string
  setup?: { agentsMd?: string; skills?: { name: string; files: Record<string, string> }[] }  // files must have 'SKILL.md'
  plugins?: Plugin[]          // from readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir)); their skills and MCP servers are added
  mcp?: string[]              // the connected servers this job gets; default none
  model?: string
  sandboxKey?: string         // sandboxPer 'user': which of the user's kept sandboxes; default the user's one for the harness
  access?: 'full' | 'read-only'  // what the agent may do; default 'full'
}
```

- `mcp`: names of the user's connected servers and of the app's own `tools`.
- `access`: `'full'`: every tool of the harness with no approval (Codex: `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`; Claude Code: `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`), for a sandbox that is the job's alone. `'read-only'`: the job's MCP tools, and reading files, so the harness reads its skills and AGENTS.md; no change to a file, and no network but the job's MCP servers. Codex: `--sandbox read-only` (its shell stays, because it reads a skill with `cat`; a command cannot write or open a connection), with the job's MCP tools approved in its `config.toml`. Claude Code: `--permission-mode dontAsk` with the tools `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Skill` and the job's MCP servers; each tool it refuses is a `permission` event. It does not hide files: the agent can read each file its user can read.
- Before the harness starts, byoa sends one MCP `initialize` from the sandbox to each of the job's servers, through the proxy. When no request reaches the proxy, the job does not start: an `error` event with code `mcp`, then `end` with `ok: false`. A server that does not answer gives an `error` event with code `mcp`, and the job runs.

Each run: the user's sandbox (resumed, or created for the first job; with `sandboxPer: 'job'`, a new one), the user's login, the pinned harness, the setup files in a new job folder, the task; then the login is taken out and the sandbox is paused (or destroyed). Stop the loop (or call `return()`) to end a job early; byoa still cleans up.

### Events (one schema for both harnesses)

```ts
type AgentEvent =
  | { type: 'start'; harness: string; version: string; sandbox: string }
  | { type: 'text'; text: string }
  | { type: 'tool_call'; id: string; name: string; server?: string; input: unknown }   // server: the MCP server
  | { type: 'tool_result'; id: string; ok: boolean; output: string }
  | { type: 'permission'; tool: string; decision: 'denied'; input?: unknown }
  | { type: 'error'; message: string; code?: 'signed-out' | 'expired' | 'harness' | 'sandbox' | 'mcp' }
  | { type: 'end'; ok: boolean; result?: string; usage?: { input: number; output: number; cached?: number; costUsd?: number } }
```

`run` does not throw for job failures: it yields `error` events and then exactly one `end`. `signed-out` / `expired`: ask the user to sign in again (`loginState` says the same). `mcp`: a server is not connected, its grant failed, it did not answer through the proxy, or the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (then the job did not start).

### session(user, { harness, setup?, plugins?, mcp?, sandboxKey?, access? }): Promise<Session>

For an app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness. Throws `LoginError` when the harness is not signed in, and `ProxyError` when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The app starts the harness itself, so `access` changes only the files byoa writes (Codex's MCP config).

```ts
const s = await agents.session(userId, { harness: 'claude', mcp: ['notion'] })
try {
  await s.sandbox.run(`my-server --claude ${s.bin}`, { cwd: s.work, env: s.env })
} finally { await s.close() }   // ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses (or destroys) the sandbox
```

`Session`: `sandbox`, `work` (the job folder with byoa's files), `harness`, `bin` (the pinned binary), `version`, `env` (login folder, `BYOA_JOB_TOKEN`, and for Claude Code `MCP_TIMEOUT`), `token`, `mcp` (`[{ name, url }]` at the proxy), `missing` (servers not connected), `failing` (`[{ name, message }]`: servers that did not answer through the proxy), `reportLogin('signed-in' | 'expired')`, `close()`.

### jobToken(user, { mcp?, ttlMs? }): Promise<JobToken>

A job token with no sandbox, for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes (such as on the user's own computer). `{ token, job, mcp, missing, close() }`. Send `token` as `Authorization: Bearer` to each `mcp[].url`.

## Store adapter

```ts
interface Entry { value: string; version: string }
interface Store {
  get(key: string): Promise<Entry | null>
  put(key: string, value: string): Promise<void>                        // writes whatever is there
  delete(key: string): Promise<void>
  cas(key: string, version: string | null, value: string): Promise<boolean>  // null: only if no entry; true if it wrote
}
```

The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant depends on `cas`.

- Postgres: run `POSTGRES_SCHEMA` once (or `postgresSchema('my_table')`), then `postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) })`.
- Convex: `convex/schema.ts` has `byoa: convexTable()`; `convex/byoa.ts` has `export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions()`; in an action or HTTP action, `store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa)`. Call byoa only from actions and HTTP actions, and serve `agents.proxy` from an HTTP action.
- Tests: `memoryStore()` from `byoa`.

## Sandbox adapter

```ts
interface SandboxProvider {
  readonly name: string
  create(opts?: { volumes?: { name: string; path: string }[]; labels?: Record<string, string>; timeoutMs?: number; keep?: boolean }): Promise<Sandbox>
  resume(id: string, opts?: { timeoutMs?: number }): Promise<Sandbox>  // starts a paused one; throws SandboxGoneError when it is gone
  destroy(id: string): Promise<void>                                   // by id, running or paused
  deleteVolume(name: string): Promise<void>
}
interface Sandbox {
  readonly id: string
  readonly home: string
  run(cmd: string, opts?: { cwd?; env?; timeoutMs?; onStdout?; onStderr?; background? }): Promise<{ exitCode; stdout; stderr }>
  writeFile(path: string, data: string | Uint8Array): Promise<void>
  pause(): Promise<void>      // keeps the files; resume starts it again
  destroy(): Promise<void>
}
```

- `keep: true`: a sandbox byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider pauses it instead of deleting it.
- E2B: `pause` takes a snapshot of the files only where the team can (`mode: 'filesystem'`), else a full one after it ends the sandbox's processes. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit.
- E2B: the default template is `byoa`; build it once per pin change with `buildE2BTemplate()`. Any template with Node 20 or later works (byoa installs the pinned harness when it is missing, more slowly).
- Daytona: `pause` stops the sandbox; `resume` starts it (also from archived, more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped.
- Daytona: with `cliLogin`, every user's login is a subpath of one shared volume (`byoa` by default). On Tier 1 and 2 a sandbox reaches only allowed domains, so serve the proxy on one (for example `*.convex.site`, `*.workers.dev`).
- Instabox: `pause` stops the sandbox; `resume` starts it, and a sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again, so no process of an earlier job runs. A kept sandbox has no time limit, and Instabox keeps it until it is deleted; a sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its `timeoutMs`. The home folder is `/data/home`. A sandbox gets none of the account's Vault items or org Secrets, and no command is in Instabox's command history. Sandboxes reach every public domain. `create` with volumes throws. The free plan allows one sandbox at a time and three starts a minute; the adapter waits for a start when Instabox answers 429.

## The fake harness

`harness: 'fake'` runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would. Each task line `call <server>.<tool> <json arguments>` is one MCP call through the real proxy; it shows the task's first line as one `text` event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the `end` event's `result`. Use it with `localSandbox()` and `memoryStore()` (or the app's own store) in tests.

---

Source: https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/README.md

# AI-native to-do list: an example app on byoa

A small to-do app. The user signs in with their own Claude or ChatGPT plan, connects their to-dos one time, and then asks the agent to change them ("add buy milk, and mark the oldest one done"). Each request is one job: byoa resumes the user's sandbox (or creates it for the first job), runs the user's own, unmodified Claude Code or Codex in it, and pauses the sandbox after the job.

The app has no code from Bookish. It is the second app for check V2 in [SPEC.md](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/SPEC.md#verification).

## The files

| File | What it does | Lines of code |
|---|---|---|
| [app.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/app.ts) | The backend, as one fetch handler. All of the app's byoa code is here. | 87 |
| [todos.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todos.ts) | The app's own data (SQLite), its MCP server with four to-do tools, and byoa's store adapter for SQLite. | 60 |
| [main.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/main.ts) | Starts the server on Node and selects the sandbox provider. | 25 |
| [page.html](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/page.html) | The page: sign in, connect, ask, and the list. | 120 |
| [todo.test.ts](https://github.com/madeyexz/byoa/blob/main/examples/todo/todo.test.ts) | Tests with byoa's fake harness. | 103 |

"Lines of code" does not count empty lines and comments.
